entry: Country in West Asia, at the southern end of the [[Arabian Peninsula]]. Its constitutional capital and largest city is [[Sanaa]], and its territory includes the Socotra Archipelago. The population is estimated at 34.7 million, predominantly Muslim Arabs. For centuries Yemen was a primary producer of [[Coffee|coffee]], exported through the port of Mokha. During the 19th century the country was divided between the [[Ottoman Empire]] and British empires. North Yemen and South Yemen were separate states until they united in 1990. [[Ali Abdullah Saleh]] served as the first president of the modern republic until his resignation in 2012, in the wake of the [[Arab Spring]]. A civil war that began in 2014 has caused a severe humanitarian crisis. In 2019 the [[United Nations]] reported that about 24 million people, nearly 75% of the population, needed humanitarian aid. Yemen is one of the least developed countries in the world.

Armed conflict in [[Yemen]] that began in late 2014, when Houthi forces took over the capital, [[Sanaa]]. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 with air strikes to restore the former government. The war is widely regarded as part of the Iran–Saudi proxy conflict, although Iran has not directly intervened. A UN-brokered truce in 2022 was extended, but fighting resumed, and the ceasefire collapsed in September and October 2026. [[Al-Qaeda]] and the [[Islamic State]] also carry out attacks. According to the UN, more than 150,000 people have been killed.

River system in [[Siberia]], the fifth-longest in the world and the largest draining into the [[Arctic Ocean]]. Beginning in [[Mongolia]], it follows a northerly course through the Krasnoyarsk Dam before draining into the Yenisei Gulf in the [[Kara Sea]]. Its basin includes [[Lake Baikal]], the world's deepest lake. The river divides the Western Siberian Plain from the Central Siberian Plateau and drains a large part of central Siberia. It is the central one of three large Siberian rivers flowing into the Arctic, the others being the [[Ob]] and the Lena. Its maximum depth is 61 meters (200 ft) and its average depth is 14 meters (45 ft). The first written mention, as "Kem," dates to the 7th century in [[Tang dynasty]] China.

South American holly species, *Ilex paraguariensis*, whose leaves are steeped in hot water to make a beverage called mate. Brewed cold, it is used to make tereré. Both the plant and the beverage contain [[Caffeine|caffeine]]. The Guaraní and some Tupi communities cultivated and drank it before [[European colonization of the Americas]]. After the [[Jesuits]] recognized its commercial potential, it spread throughout the province and elsewhere in the Spanish Crown. Mate is traditionally consumed in central and southern South America, and bottled and canned iced drinks are now sold worldwide.

Capital and largest city of [[Armenia]] (pop., 2022: 1,086,677), on the Hrazdan River. One of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities, it was founded as the fortress of Erebuni in 782 BC by King Argishti I of [[Urartu]]. The city was mostly depopulated by the Great Surgun of 1603–05, when the Safavid Empire deported hundreds of thousands of Armenians to [[Iran]], and an earthquake in 1679 mostly destroyed it. It came under the [[Russian Empire]] in 1828. After World War I it became the capital of the First Republic of Armenia, and thousands of survivors of the [[Armenian genocide]] arrived. Under [[Soviet Union|Soviet]] rule it grew into the country's cultural and industrial center. Landmarks include Saint Gregory Cathedral, the largest Armenian cathedral in the world, and the Matenadaran, which holds one of the largest collections of ancient books and manuscripts. [[UNESCO]] named Yerevan World Book Capital in 2012.

Gram-negative, non-motile bacterium that causes [[Plague (disease)|plague]]. Its main route to humans is the bite of the oriental rat flea, *Xenopsylla cheopis*, and it also infects rodents and other mammals. Alexandre Yersin identified it in 1894, during a plague epidemic in Hong Kong. The bacterium caused two of the deadliest pandemics in recorded history, the Plague of Justinian and the [[Black Death]]. Between one thousand and two thousand human cases are still reported each year to the [[World Health Organization]].

English progressive rock band, formed in London in 1968. Founded by Jon Anderson, Chris Squire, Bill Bruford, Tony Kaye and Peter Banks, Yes was widely regarded as a pioneer of progressive rock. Four consecutive albums, from *The Yes Album* (1971) to the live *Yessongs* (1973), sold platinum or multi-platinum in the United States. Their 1983 album *90125* featured their only US number-one single, "Owner of a Lonely Heart." The band was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2017. Squire died in 2015, and the latest album, *Aurora*, was released in June 2026.

Large, hairy, mythical humanoid said to inhabit the [[Himalayas]]. Also called the Abominable Snowman in Western popular culture, it is often compared with [[Bigfoot]] of North America. The name derives from Tibetan words for rocky place and bear. Folklorists trace the legend to Sherpa folklore and to misidentified animals such as [[Bear|bears]] and [[Yak|yaks]]. Sightings, photographs and footprint casts have been offered as evidence, but some are hoaxes. A 2017 analysis by Charlotte Lindqvist of the University at Buffalo found that supposed Yeti hairs and bones belonged to known bears.

Immense sacred tree at the center of Norse cosmology, around which the Nine Worlds exist. It is described in the [[Poetic Edda]] and in the Prose Edda of [[Snorri Sturluson]], both compiled in the 13th century. The gods gather beneath it daily at their governing assemblies. Three roots reach to the well Urðarbrunnr in the heavens, the spring Hvergelmir and the well Mímisbrunnr. Creatures living in the tree include the dragon Níðhöggr, the squirrel Ratatoskr and the hawk Veðrfölnir. The name is generally taken to mean "Odin's horse," in the sense of gallows, though scholars disagree.

Korean admiral of the Joseon period, renowned for his victories over the Japanese navy in the [[Imjin War]]. He is generally credited with at least 23 naval battles, all of them victories, many fought while his forces were outnumbered and poorly supplied. At the Battle of Myeongnyang he led a fleet of 13 ships against a Japanese fleet of at least 133. He was posthumously honored with the title Lord of Loyal Valor. Yi was killed by a gunshot wound at the Battle of Noryang, the last major battle of the Imjin War. His wartime journals, the *Nanjung Ilgi*, are part of the [[UNESCO]] Memory of the World initiative, and landmarks, awards and towns in Korea bear his name.

West Germanic language historically spoken by Ashkenazi Jews. It originated in the [[Holy Roman Empire]] during the Middle Ages, with a vernacular based on High German, fused with many elements from Hebrew and Aramaic and with some [[Slavic languages|Slavic]] and Romance vocabulary. It has traditionally been written in the [[Hebrew alphabet]]. Before World War II the language still had 11–13 million speakers, and about 85% of the approximately six million Jews murdered in the [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]] spoke Yiddish, causing a massive decline in its use. Today most daily speakers are Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) Jews, and a 2021 estimate from Rutgers University counted 600,000 speakers worldwide. Eastern Yiddish is far more common than Western Yiddish.

Pair of complementary cosmic principles in Chinese philosophy. Yin is retractive, passive and receptive, while yang is active, expansive and repelling, and the two interact so that the whole is greater than its parts. The concept originated in ancient China, and its dualities appear in natural processes from seasons to landscapes. Taiji, the Supreme Ultimate, is the undifferentiated state from which yin and yang arise. The organization of [[Qi|qi]], the material energy of the universe, forms the 10 thousand things between Heaven and Earth. The idea underlies [[Traditional Chinese medicine]], the [[I Ching]] and Chinese martial arts such as [[Baguazhang]], and it is central to [[Taoism]] and [[Confucianism]].

Israeli general and statesman, prime minister in 1974–1977 and 1992–1995. Born in Jerusalem, Rabin rose through the Palmach and the [[Israel Defense Forces]], becoming chief of the general staff in 1964; he oversaw Israel's victory in the [[Six-Day War]]. In his second term he signed the [[Oslo Accords]] with the [[Palestine Liberation Organization]]. In 1994 he shared the Nobel Peace Prize with [[Shimon Peres]] and [[Yasser Arafat]], and he also signed a peace treaty with Jordan that year. He was shot dead in Tel Aviv by Yigal Amir, an opponent of the accords, who was sentenced to life imprisonment.

Group of physical, mental and spiritual practices that originated in ancient India. Aimed at controlling body and mind to attain liberation, or moksha, yoga is practiced in Hindu, [[Jainism|Jain]] and [[Buddhism|Buddhist]] traditions. It is first attested in the early first millennium BCE, and systematic concepts emerged in the fifth and sixth centuries BCE among ascetic movements including Jainism and Buddhism. The Yoga Sutras of [[Patanjali]], the classical text on Hindu yoga, date to the early centuries of the [[Common Era]]. Hatha yoga texts emerged between the ninth and 11th centuries, originating in [[Tantra]]. Much Western yoga is a modern form built largely on asanas, or postures, derived from hatha yoga and Western physical culture, while traditional yoga emphasizes meditation. [[Swami Vivekananda]] introduced the Yoga Sutras to the West in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

Food produced by bacterial fermentation of milk, also spelled yoghurt. Bacteria ferment the sugars in milk into [[Lactic acid|lactic acid]], which acts on the milk protein to give yogurt its texture and tart flavor. Most yogurt is made from cow's [[Milk|milk]], though milk from water buffalo, goats, camels and [[Yak|yaks]] can also be used. The main bacteria are *Lactobacillus delbrueckii* subsp. *bulgaricus* and *Streptococcus thermophilus*. The most widely accepted view is that yogurt emerged when nomads carried milk in animal-skin bags. The earliest archaeological evidence of dairying from the [[Neolithic]] period, at Barcın Höyük in northwest Turkey, dates to 6600 BCE. The word derives from Ottoman Turkish. Greek yogurt, strained to remove whey, contains about twice the protein of regular yogurt.

Capital of the Special Region of Yogyakarta, on the island of [[Java]] in [[Indonesia]] (pop., 2020: 373,589). It is the only Indonesian royal city still ruled by a monarchy, and it is regarded as a center of classical Javanese arts such as batik, wayang puppetry and silversmithing. Yogyakarta was the Indonesian capital from 1946 to 1948 during the [[Indonesian National Revolution]]. It is home to Gadjah Mada University, the country's largest institute of higher education. Its name, meaning roughly fit to prosper, refers to Ayodhya, the birthplace of Rama in the [[Ramayana]]. The city has a score of 0.887 on the [[Human Development Index]], the highest of any Indonesian regency or city.

Emperor of Ethiopia (r. 1871–1889), formerly king of Tigray. He rebelled against [[Tewodros II]] in the 1860s and later assisted the British expedition to Abyssinia that ended in Tewodros's suicide, receiving ammunition and artillery in return. He defended Ethiopia against a large-scale [[Egypt|Egyptian]] invasion and clashed with [[Muhammad Ahmad]] during the Mahdist War. Yohannes regarded [[Islam]] as a hindrance to the stability of the state and worked to strengthen Christian dominance; he is estimated to have forcibly converted 550,000 Oromos and Jebertis. He was killed at the Battle of Gallabat, and a succession dispute followed involving [[Menelik II]].

Japanese-born artist, musician and peace activist. Her work includes performance art and filmmaking, and she was active in New York's downtown art scene in the early 1960s, including the Fluxus group. In 1969 she married [[John Lennon]] of the Beatles, and the couple staged bed-ins as public protests against the Vietnam War. Their album *Double Fantasy* (1980) won the Grammy Award for Album of the Year. After Lennon's murder that year, she funded the Strawberry Fields memorial in [[Central Park]] and the Imagine Peace Tower in Iceland.

Second-largest city in Japan and capital of Kanagawa Prefecture (pop., 2023: 3.7 million). It lies on Tokyo Bay, south of [[Tokyo]], in the Kantō region of Honshu, and is the major economic and cultural hub of the Greater Tokyo Area. Yokohama was one of the cities opened to Western trade after Japan's policy of seclusion ended in 1859, and it developed into a cosmopolitan port city. Foreigners first occupied the low-lying Kannai district. Today the city is home to headquarters of companies including [[Nissan]] and Isuzu, and landmarks include Minato Mirai 21 and Yokohama Chinatown.

Holiest day of the Jewish year, the Day of Atonement. Observed on the 10th of Tishrei in the [[Hebrew calendar]], in late September or early October, it centers on atonement and repentance. Traditional observance includes a full fast, extended prayer services at the [[Synagogue|synagogue]] and confession of sins. It is one of the two High Holy Days, with Rosh Hashanah, and the last of the Ten Days of Repentance. The [[Torah]] prohibits work on the day. When the Temple in Jerusalem stood, a sacrificial service included a lottery drawn on two goats; the goat sent to Azazel was driven off a cliff, the origin of the term scapegoat.

1973 war between Israel and a coalition of Arab states led by [[Egypt]] and Syria. Launched on October 6, 1973, during the Jewish holy day of Yom Kippur, it was fought mainly in the [[Sinai Peninsula]] and the [[Golan Heights]], territories Israel had occupied in 1967. Egyptian forces crossed the Suez Canal, and Israel pushed back the Syrians and counterattacked. The [[Soviet Union]] and the United States conducted large resupply efforts. Ceasefires on October 22 and 25 ended the fighting. The war contributed to the 1978 Camp David Accords, under which Israel returned the Sinai to Egypt, and to an Egypt–Israel peace treaty.

Third emperor of the [[Ming dynasty]] of China (r. 1402–1424), personal name Zhu Di. The fourth son of the [[Hongwu Emperor]], he was made Prince of Yan in 1370 and based himself in Beiping, now [[Beijing]], to guard the northern frontier. After a three-year civil war against his nephew, the Jianwen Emperor, he seized the throne. Construction of a new capital from 1407 to 1420, including the [[Forbidden City]], employed hundreds of thousands of workers. He sponsored the *Yongle Encyclopedia*, which employed around two thousand scholars. Maritime expeditions led by [[Zheng He]] reached Southeast Asia, India, Persia and East Africa.

South Korean politician who served as president from 2022 until his removal in 2025. A former prosecutor general, he narrowly defeated Democratic Party nominee Lee Jae Myung by less than a percentage point in 2022. On December 3, 2024, he declared martial law, the first such declaration since the military dictatorship of Chun Doo-hwan in 1980. The National Assembly voted to nullify it within hours, and the Constitutional Court unanimously upheld his impeachment in April 2025. In February 2026 he was sentenced to [[Life imprisonment|life imprisonment]] for leading an insurrection.

Cathedral city in North Yorkshire, England, with Roman origins. Founded as the fortress settlement of Eboracum in AD 71, it later became the capital of Deira, Northumbria and Scandinavian York. In the Middle Ages it was the center of the northern English ecclesiastical province and a wool-trading hub. Its minster, castle and city walls are all Grade I listed. The city became a major railway hub in the 19th century and was bombed in the Baedeker Blitz during World War II. Its built-up area had 141,685 residents at the 2021 census.

Historic county of northern England, named after the city of [[York]]. Formerly the largest county in the United Kingdom by area, it was divided into North, East and West ridings. Its southwest includes [[Leeds]] and [[Sheffield]], and the Yorkshire Dales lie in the Pennines. In 1974 the historic county was divided among four modern ceremonial counties. Its emblem is the white rose, originally the heraldic badge of the Plantagenet House of York. Yorkshire Day is observed each year on August 1.
